blocks.text: Then we had reached the handover at the end of the night shift into the day shift of 10 June 2015. That's tile or still 287. I think we'd actually got to 290, but if we start at 287, just to contextualise where we'd reached.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Got there? Three-quarters of the way along the scroll bar.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mrs Hocknell, I think yesterday you had told us about the material in the nursing notes relating to the handover. So as we see there on the screen, tile 287 represents the nursing notes made by [Nurse A] --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: -- who had been the designated nurse for [Baby B] on the night shift.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: We went behind that, as indeed I believe we went behind 288, which is material written by Laura Eagles, who's the day shift designated nurse on 10 June.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: It simply relates to her taking over care of [Baby B] at 8 am?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: And it's a note she wrote towards the end of the shift at 17.52?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we go to 289 then, please, and just deal with this? If we can go behind that, please. It's a note relating to what happened at 8.09. Can you deal with that, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is a note made by [Nurse A]:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Parents had gone to ward to sleep. Asked to be called if anything changed. Contacted after doctors called to attend and arrived shortly afterwards. Kept updated throughout. Very upset and have remained on unit throughout the night since with maternal grandparents for support. Mum has slept in recliner for a few hours and dad has slept for periods in parents' accommodation. Updated re D-dimer this morning by Dr Lambie and though glad to have the start of an answer are understandably upset too. Mum became very upset blaming herself because of her own clotting disorder."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. The next still is 290, which we're becoming familiar, I think, with the system now. It is the hourly observations, this time at 10 minutes past the hour, but we have the usual collection of the observation chart, the intensive care chart and the equipment settings.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: So that triptych, if you like, of pictures. Then a further nursing update made by [Nurse A] from the night shift.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: We put this in because it's timestamped by the system as having been made at that time.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: What does it read, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Nil by mouth since midnight due to resus and ventilation."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: So that's a reference to, just to put that in context, to the fact that liquid feeds through the mouth, through the oral route, had been stopped because of what had happened?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then at 8.31, some blood gas records. At 8.48, the collection of some blood, a blood sample. Is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: We'll leave that for the doctors. Then the blood test results at 8.59. Then at 9 am, Dr Saladi, the on-duty consultant, did a ward round and there is a note of his examination of [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Can we deal with that, please? Is this your typed transposition of what is written in the notes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we deal with it, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Events overnight noted. 31 plus 2. Day 4."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Which is then corrected to 31 plus 5:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "M morphine [medication morphine], teicoplanin, cefotaxime, caffeine, nystatin. Fluids TPN 90ml/kg. On examination: pink, well perfused. Capillary refill time 2 seconds and fontanelle soft. HS 1 plus 2 plus 0. No murmur. Abdo: soft not tender."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then there's a drawing in the notes:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "D-dimer 6210. Discussion with parents. ?why she had acute episode overnight. Explained that D-dimer is raised ? in babies more commonly related to DIC.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Two-hourly (sic) to injection rather than clotting abnormally."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Is that "secondary to"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Secondary to, sorry.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Secondary to injection rather than clotting abnormally. We will discuss with Alder Hey plus NNU in Liverpool. Supportive treatment for the baby. Plan: repeat CRUS [cranial ultrasound scan], continue with antibiotics, discussion with specialists at Alder Hey and NNU at Liverpool regards events overnight."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Yes. Then there's a record of his observations.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Sometimes these notes are written by one of the junior doctors who is with the specialist, with the consultant; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: And sometimes they're in the consultant's own handwriting?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Can we go back to events, please? Still at 10 past the hour, we have the three separate sets of readings.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then we go to the three same separate sets of readings, but defaulting back to on the hour at --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Further clinical notes of Dr Sally Ogden, one of the -- I think she is a registrar, is she, ST3?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: ST3, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: That's the bottom grade of registrar in effect. Can we go to those, please? I'm not going to ask you to read these out because we will deal with them with the witness. All right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Now we've established what the system is. But you have there typed out what she has written in her legible handwriting?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you, all right. And of course the handwriting is behind.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can we go back to events then, please. Then what's classified as medication, sodium chloride, saline solution?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: And caffeine at 10.33, which is signed and countersigned by Laura Eagles and Christopher Booth.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Carry on, please. The observation charts again at 11 o'clock, which we've seen before.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: The observation chart is repeated at midday?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: And then of course Lucy Letby had gone off duty -- her shift had ended formally at 8 o'clock. At 12.04 we have a series of messages between her and Jennifer Jones-Key.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think these have been already read through by you in the context --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think this might be different.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: I was wondering whether it was just my memory. Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Let's deal with this because this is different, I think.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm relying on your memory. Thanks.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 12.04 a WhatsApp message is sent by Lucy Letby to Jennifer Jones-Key:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Been for breakfast with [Nurse E]. Feel quite awake now. Going to unpack a bit and [wash] uniform. Hope your day okay. Will you let me know if any change with [Baby B], please."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then there are a series of WhatsApp messages of a social nature between Lucy Letby and Minna Lappalainen between 12.29 and 12.40 hours.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The observations of [Baby B] continued. A blood gas record just before 1 o'clock and then the habitual observations on the hour. Further saline, sodium chloride, at 1.30, nystatin and cefotaxime.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: At 2 o'clock, as before, some readings. Then a clinical note at 2 pm -- or two sets of clinical notes. The first from Dr Sally Ogden, the registrar. If we just look at that, please. That's just setting out what is going on, so further discussion with haematology, so they're investigating the blood issue, potential blood issue, I should say.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then back to events, please. Dr Brearey, not to be confused with [Nurse A], who is one of the nurses, [Nurse A]. Dr Stephen Brearey is one of the consultants. Just click on that, please. That relates to a review that he undertook of [Baby B]'s heart, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Again, I'm not going to ask you to read that out, other than to remark on the fact that everything appeared to be normal.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Back, please. Again, no doubt delayed because Dr Brearey was examining [Baby B] at 2 o'clock, the observations at 14.10. Then resumed at 15.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: At 16.00 hours, the same?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then some nursing notes relating to events at 4 pm. Can we just deal with those, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Nursed on SIMV 20/6. Weaned to 18/6 at 16.00. Rate initially increased from 25 beats per minute to 40 as CO2 rising. Has since weaned to 30 on capillary blood gas results. ET suction not needed. Op suction yielding clear secretions. Air entry equal and clear."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. The observation chart is again at 5 pm?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Dr Ogden's notes at 5 pm also, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This relates to the report from the pathologist, who had conducted a post-mortem examination of [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Can we focus on the final paragraph where recorded is "no obvious cause of death found".
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we return, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Blood gas record at 17.07?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Further medication administered and countersigned by Laura Eagles and Belinda Simcock?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: And the nursing notes -- the time that the nursing notes have been made to cover the day was 17.52?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Can we just turn to those, please? And again, this is further detail of material that we've seen in other people's notes in effect.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, and also outlined at 8 o'clock and 4 pm.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Yes. Thank you. Can we go back to events, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is a message to Lucy Letby at 18.31 from Jennifer Jones- Key.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct. She writes:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Day manic and got a 30 weekend vented. No change with [Baby B] when I had left."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: It may be that autocorrect had corrected "weeker" to "weekend".
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: That may be an explanation for why it says "weekend".
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then at 19.11, Lucy Letby replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Oh dear."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "It's okay, six on all week now and Yvonne F doing an on-call."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Good, hope you're okay. W."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Yeah, just tired. Did feeds, ROP and 5 resus with parents and 6 lots of baby massage. Working Friday now."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: And follows that up with:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Hope you are okay."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Wow, well done. Had a few hours with Minna this aft and walk into town. Just had shower and going to chill."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Sounds good to me."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby then sends a message to [Nurse A] at 22.09:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "How is [Baby B]?"
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: [Nurse A] replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Looks really good. Wanted her vented overnight but blocked her tube and happy on CPAP. Not that that means anything after last night!"
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then she follows up with:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "We also have a 30/40 [or 30-weeker] 800-gram and new 31/40 twins. T1 girl. T2 boy. Boy vented and in [Baby A]'s space. Other two newbies on CPAP."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Further message sent:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "[Baby A]'s prelim report. No gross abnormalities.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: So [no] bleeds, clots or line issues. [Baby B], all ultrasound normal. D-dimer result not significant. So no idea what's happened."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Hmm, a lot of Qs still to be answered then. I so hope it isn't due to the line for [Baby A] and that [Baby B] is okay."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby follows that up:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "They've had a busy day then!"
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: [Nurse A] replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "The twins arrived for us on handover."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: And further says:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "It said no line issues. They'd have been visible if there were."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Oh I misread what you put, thought you meant no abnormalities, so looking at lines, clots, et cetera."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: She further writes:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "At least that's a positive but think we all need answers."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: That's 22.45 on 10 June.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Slightly under an hour later, 50-odd minutes later, she searched for [Mother of Babies A & B], [Baby B] and [Baby A]'s mum, on Facebook.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: That's 10 June. We then skip 2 days to Friday, 12 June.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Could you take that up, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So on 12 June there are nine text messages between Lucy Letby and Ashleigh Hudson about [Baby A] and [Baby B], which -- the full contents of which is in [Baby A]'s sequence of events.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Yes. We then have marked for contextual purposes an event concerning [Baby C] just before midnight when we can see, from the blue rim to the tile, the blue edging to the tile, Lucy Letby was on duty.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: [Baby C]'s death at just before 6 am, towards the end of that night shift, 13 to 14 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then 8 days later, events concerning [Baby D] in the early hours of 22 June at 1.30, 3 o'clock, 3.45 and then [Baby D]’s death at 4.25.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Again, on the shift where Lucy Letby was present?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: So that's 22 June, the Monday, the death of [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: On Thursday, 25th, at 21.50 what do we see?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We have another Facebook search for [Mother of Babies A & B].
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Then on the Saturday, the 27th, there's some more WhatsApp messages, aren't there?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, at 13.33 hours, Minna Lappalainen sends a text message to Lucy Letby:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Okay. We'll try to have a chat at work?"
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Honestly Minna, I shouldn't have asked. Just concentrate on the move. I'll be fine."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby follows this up with:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "I don't want to talk about it like this. I'm fine today. The last week or so has just been a bit tough, but I'm off from Friday so all will be okay."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Later that afternoon, indeed within a few --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Minutes, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: -- within 4 minutes of that WhatsApp, there's then a text from Lucy Letby to [Nurse E]; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Ha ha, nodding off in cinema isn't a good look! I had a mini meltdown last night about what's happened at work and thinking about Walton, et cetera. I just need some time off with mum and dad."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then this is an entry that I've made as a descriptive:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "[Baby B]'s medical records indicate that [Baby B] continued to receive care in the neonatal unit until she was discharged on 09/07/2015."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. That's Thursday, 9 July. Sunday the 12th, we have some more WhatsApp messaging.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There were some further WhatsApp messages between Lucy Letby and Jennifer Jones-Key about [Baby B] and her discharge home.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then the next tile, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then on Tuesday, 14 July, there is a conversation between Lucy Letby and [Nurse A] about [Baby B] and her discharge home.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. So that's a Tuesday, so 1 day short of 3 weeks later, we then have the [Baby E] event.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Just to remind the jury, the one at 9 pm is the blood round the mouth episode. [Baby E], of course, died, as shown by these stills, at 01.40 that morning.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: And we have on the following day, Wednesday, 5 August, the insulin incident involving his twin, [Baby F].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Following that, the next entry is almost a month later, 4 weeks precisely later, Wednesday, 2 September. Did Lucy Letby search for [Mother of Babies A & B] again?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then 17 days later on Saturday, 19 September, was there some further WhatsApp conversation between Lucy Letby and [Nurse A] about [Baby B]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Does that conclude the sequence of events for [Baby B]?

blocks.text: This is a statement, members of the jury, dated 5 December 2019. It begins with this:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am a consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist and currently the clinical lead for gynaecology at the Countess of Chester Hospital. I am a member of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I commenced my role as a consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist at the Countess of Chester Hospital in April 2011. My main role at the Countess of Chester Hospital is both in obstetrics and gynaecology. I have patients booked under me antenatally and I review them in the antenatal clinic, labour ward and post-natally.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I have been asked to provide a statement about my care of [Mother of Babies A & B].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I make this statement with reference to my medical notes. I have no recollection of the delivery of [Mother of Babies A & B]'s twins, but I do have some recollection of her maternal history and some of the intensive input of care that [Mother of Babies A & B] received.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] was booked under our care at the Countess of Chester Hospital."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Her hospital number reference is given:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "This was her first pregnancy and she had a twin pregnancy. She was a high-risk antenatal patient and had very extensive antenatal care provided by my colleagues. She was not booked under my care but under one of my fellow consultant colleagues here within the department. My colleagues had liaised extensively with colleagues in London as she did have increased risk factors in her pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] was diagnosed with antiphospholipid syndrome, a clotting abnormality. [Mother of Babies A & B] was on long-term warfarin and under the care of University College London Hospital. On [Mother of Babies A & B]'s first antenatal visit there had been extensive discussion that she was at increased risk, because of her medical conditions, for preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, due to a raised BMI of 45, and she was at risk of venous thromboembolism, a blood clot in her leg or lung.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "With regard to the foetuses, there was risk of intrauterine growth restriction, foetal loss, and preterm labour with early delivery.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] was aware that she was a high-risk pregnancy and she was on low-dose molecular weight heparin and aspirin throughout. I was aware that she had been admitted to the ward for observation from 29 weeks and 3 days on 25 May 2015."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That of course is a reference to her gestational state/stage:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "This was because she had shown an increased amount of protein in her urine and her blood pressure had become slightly increased and labile, requiring her to go on an oral antihypertensive medication and receive intramuscular steroids to assist with foetal lung maturation in the event of early delivery.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My first physical contact with [Mother of Babies A & B] was when I was consultant on call for the day. She had been an inpatient for a number of weeks and I first met her as a patient on 7 June 2015 when she was 31 weeks and 2 days. On that day I was working with a senior experienced registrar.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As [Mother of Babies A & B] had dichorionic diamniotic twins and a high-risk pregnancy, there had already been quite an extensive plan put in place by the consultants that were directly looking after her. We were concerned that she was developing a condition called pre-eclampsia, where her blood pressure would go up and therefore there was a potential of going on to develop eclampsia, where she could potentially fit.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The planning in her notes detailed that if there was a deterioration in her blood results, if she became symptomatic for pre-eclampsia or if her blood pressure rose above 160/100 on two occasions then we were to consider delivery. I believe [Mother of Babies A & B] was aware of this plan.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I had reviewed her earlier that day on the ward at 12.10 hours, having noted and written her blood results in the previous day. [Mother of Babies A & B]'s liver function was raised but had been stable and her blood pressure was stable so my plan had been to continue her care as per my consultant colleagues: performing daily bloods and monitoring her blood pressure.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The registrar contacted me later on in the afternoon, around about 17.17 hours, telling me that there had been a deterioration in her blood results, a number of them had increased and some had decreased, and there had also been a rise in her blood pressure.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The decision was taken at that stage that she should be transferred from the ward directly down to our central labour suite, which is a safer environment for one-to-one care. That was so that we could try to help to stabilise her blood pressure.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I came directly to the labour ward. The babies' heart rate was recorded with a CTG machine, and their monitoring was satisfactory throughout. Our efforts were concentrated on stabilising [Mother of Babies A & B].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We then liaised with a number of staff members.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The staff involved in caring for [Mother of Babies A & B] at this time were myself, the senior registrar Dr Finney, and midwifery staff. At the time we would have been gaining venous access in order to take further bloods from mother and we placed her directly on a drug called magnesium sulphate, which helps to prevent mothers having a fit and going on to develop eclampsia.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "If there was an escalation in her pre-eclamptic features she potentially could go on and fit. We also asked the anaesthetist to come and review her. We put [Mother of Babies A & B] on the pre-eclampsia protocol, for which there is a high dependency chart with frequent measures of her blood pressure. She was catheterised to measure her urine output and she was fluid restricted.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This was all in an effort to prevent her condition worsening and developing eclampsia.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I discussed the situation with the anaesthetist and haematologist because [Mother of Babies A & B] was on low molecular weight heparin, which is to help to thin her blood due to the APS. We prepared [Mother of Babies A & B] for theatre by having her blood cross-matched and specific blood infusions that we use in theatre to help the uterus to contract, all to minimise blood loss for her were we to go ahead and deliver her.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her blood pressure was not adequately stable and we were further required to give her anti-hypertensive medication intravenously to help to bring her blood pressure down as it remained high. We made the decision at 18.15 hours to deliver her because of this instability and worsening pre-eclampsia.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We obtained verbal and handwritten consent from [Mother of Babies A & B]. We worked to optimise her into a more stable condition, informing the people who had to be there, the anaesthetist, the haematologist, and the neonatal team. The
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: babies had already received steroid injections to help with the lung maturation because of prematurity.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Once we had liaised with everyone, stabilised [Mother of Babies A & B], and had all the team present, we transferred her into the theatre at 19.45 hours. In the theatre, there would have been two anaesthetists, two midwives, one each to take the baby, the paediatric team.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: There would have been two neonatal Resuscitaires in the room and each of them would be staffed by independent neonatal staff. Myself, my assistant and a theatre scrub nurse were also present. We also had the additional assistance of the senior house officer.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There would also have been an operating department practitioner to assist the anaesthetic staff. The anaesthetist had contacted his consultant as well.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her blood pressure was very markedly raised in theatre, so we had to further stabilise her and give her further intravenous anti-hypertensive medication to bring her blood pressure down. The anaesthetic team put in specific lines, arterial lines, to help assist them in their management of her blood pressure. The general anaesthetic was commenced around about 20.17 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Although the decision (inaudible) for delivery was made at 18.15 hours, the general anaesthetic was not commenced until 20.17 hours because our priority was to stabilise [Mother of Babies A & B] as there was a risk that she might have a significant fall in her blood pressure once the babies and the placenta were delivered.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I then commenced the procedure. I was the lead surgeon and my assistant was Dr Finney. One of the senior house officers, Dr Batt(?), additionally assisted in theatre.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Knife to skin, the start of the operation, was at 20.25 hours and I delivered twin 1 at 20.30 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Twin 1 was the female twin and she was passed directly to the paediatric resus and neonatal team.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I delivered twin number 2 at 20.31 hours and passed him directly to the neonatal team at the paediatric resus station. That was the end of my contact with the babies.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Twin 1 was a cephalic, head down presentation, an easy delivery, and passed directly to the paediatricians. Twin 2 had been lying transverse, but I delivered him through breach
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: techniques, which is routine for delivery of a transverse lie, and passed him directly to the paediatricians.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It is documented that this was a routine caesarean section. There were no complications and minimal blood loss of 700 millilitres. My concentration at the time of the cesarean section was on delivering the babies and passing them safely across to the midwife. The midwife then transfers them across to the paediatric resus and neonatal team. I would have clamped and cut the cord of the first baby, allowing transfer to the neonatal team, whilst I dealt with the next baby, cut the cord and transferred it also directly across.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The babies were only in my hands for a matter of seconds and I did not make any assessment as to the condition of them, the babies. It was an uncomplicated, routine, straightforward delivery. [Mother of Babies A & B] would then have been transferred back on to one of our labour ward high dependency rooms.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was on call until 8.30 hours on 8 June 2015, during which time I saw [Mother of Babies A & B] and the babies' father for a debriefing.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Post-operatively, the babies would have been on the neonatal unit and mum and dad would have been on the central labour suite, but with access to go through directly. [Mother of Babies A & B] was subsequently discharged home a number of days later and had a post-natal review some 6 weeks later by her consultant who had administered the antenatal care.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am aware that [Baby A] had, sadly, died on 8 June 2015. I am not sure how I heard about this, whether it was from a formal meeting or otherwise.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I was unaware that [Baby B] had suffered a collapse at the hospital."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: There were some medical terms in that statement, some of which the jury will have been familiar with. I am sure that most women and a lot of men would know about eclampsia and pre-eclampsia and the risks of eclampsia, but there were others that I hadn't heard of before. I don't think it's important. People needn't worry about those. Anything that requires any definition, it'll be in the glossary. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The next statement was made by a midwife called Rachel Wright. She made her statement on 11 March 2019 and informed us that she is a band 6 midwife at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She, in her work, would only look after women if they came into hospital and usually working on ward 32, which is the post-natal ward where mothers and babies would go after delivery. This ward also accommodates mums who also require medical attention when they are pregnant. Examples of this could be not feeling the baby move frequently, having a bleed or even being involved in a car accident. Initially, mums would attend the labour ward and if their medical condition needed monitoring they would then be moved to ward 32 to be cared for until they were fit to leave:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have been asked to provide details of my involvement with [Babies A & B] and their mother, [Mother of Babies A & B]. From memory, I do not recall my involvement. I have used the maternity notes that I made during my shift on the 7th into 8 June 2015 to assist me.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 7 June 2015, I was known as Rachel Hope. I was working on the labour ward on a night shift. Back in June 2015, the night shift would start at 8 pm and would finish at 8.30 am, the following day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When we come on duty at 8 pm we would go into the office and all stand around a board with all the ladies' names and details relating to their labour. We would get allocated a patient each, then have a safety briefing. After the briefing, we would head off to our patients and take over from the midwife who had been looking after them. Once we meet our patient we receive a more in-depth handover from the midwife who had been on the day shift.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On the evening of this night shift, 7 June 2015, I can see from the notes that there was no handover, like I have just described, as I went straight down to theatre about 20.10 hours. I would have left the initial handover and headed to get changed into some scrubs, which consist of top and trousers, which are cleaned especially at the hospital, and a hair net.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It looks as if my first entry on the notes is at 20.30 hours. I arrived after the first baby was born, which was [Baby B]. The second twin, [Baby A], was born at 20.31 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I would have gone into the theatre and over to the table where [Mother of Babies A & B] was having her caesarean section and the scrub nurse would have handed me a large sterile piece of paper to put over my arms to take the baby, and then Hannah Blake would have had one too as it was a twin delivery. Hannah
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Blake is the midwife who was looking after [Mother of Babies A & B] during the day shift.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We would have been at the side of the table waiting for the babies to be born. Hannah would have given me a verbal handover about what had taken place prior to my arrival. I cannot recall who else was in the room.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: There would have been a double resuscitation team also there, one for each baby at different tables in corners of the theatre. This is the norm when twins are being born, especially as these babies were very preterm. The resuscitation teams are there as a precautionary measure.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There would have been quite a lot of people in theatre due to the twins being early and mum had high blood pressure and was on medication for that. Once the twins were delivered, Hannah and I had taken a baby each to the resuscitation team. I do not know which baby I had. The notes also do not say.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At 20.33 hours, according to the notes, I had taken some blood from the placenta. This would have been taken from the veins and arteries in two syringes. This would have happened at the opposite side of the theatre.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The surgeons would have put the placenta in a pot on the table and I would have taken some bloods with a syringe.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The reason I would have done it is because there had been an emergency caesarean, so we have to take blood from the cord to ensure oxygen levels in the blood were okay for the babies at the time they were delivered.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I would have given the bloods to either my shift leader or another midwife, asking them to put the blood through the analysis machine, so I didn't have to leave theatre. They would have then brought me the results on a piece of paper. The results, according to the notes, show that there was good oxygen levels as the babies were born.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I actually remember looking over to the two resuscitation tables and I remember Hannah Blake giving CPR to [Baby B]. I remember being shocked as we were not expecting [Baby B] to have this kind of intervention.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby A] was fine.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The babies then went through to the neonatal baby unit with the teams. [Baby A] would have been wrapped up well, the baby having oxygen on his face as he was so premature, but it was the little girl, [Baby B], that I remember having any treatment.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The next entry I have written was at 21.50 hours when we had come out of theatre, so in between these times I had most probably been looking through the notes, making sure I had not missed much from the handover and getting the paperwork ready.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After theatre, [Mother of Babies A & B] was returned back to her room. During the rest of my shift until the handover the next morning, I cared for [Mother of Babies A & B] on the labour ward. I cannot remember anything significant about the shift. The notes show that I have reported to [Mother of Babies A & B] and her partner that the babies were doing well in the neonatal unit and I have recorded normal entries regarding [Mother of Babies A & B]'s observations throughout the shift.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My notes show that I went through to the baby unit at 23.30 hours for an update on the babies. At 23.55 hours, dad had gone through to the unit to check on the babies too. I have updated the parents again at 04.30 and 06.30 hours. I may have just telephoned the unit and verbally asked about the babies at these times.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At 8 am on 8 June 2015, I handed the care of [Mother of Babies A & B] over the next day to a midwife called Carolyn O'Donnell. I don't recall any other involvement in the care of [Mother of Babies A & B] or the babies and there is nothing in the notes to say that I have."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, Mr Driver, I wasn't paying close attention. Did you tell the jury the date that statement was made?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That's why both the midwife and the consultants are saying they don't have a recollection because they were talking about events 4 years before.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: They are. I remind the jury, that statement was made on 11 March 2019.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So this will have been one of many such procedures that they've gone through. So they didn't have much of an independent, if any, recollection of the event and they're relying on the notes they made at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, the next statement in terms of chronology of events at the hospital is Dr Beech.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Your Lordship has been provided with a copy of this statement, although not within the bundle.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I have it, thank you. I/575.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR GAIL KARA BEECH (read)
That's the one, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This is dated 30 April 2019, so again just short of 4 years later.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am Dr Gail Kara Beech. I qualified as a doctor in 2010 and commenced my training in paediatrics in August 2012. I have been asked to provide a statement detailing my involvement in the care of [Babies A & B]. I have had access to a copy of their clinical records to assist me along with my personal recollection of the events.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have also used the report that I originally prepared for the coroner on approximately 29 February 2016, which relates solely to [Baby A]. Some minor amendments were made to this report and I was asked about my involvement with his sister, [Baby B]."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Beech states that she worked at the Countess of Chester Hospital from 3 September 2014 to 1 September 2015:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I worked on the children's ward and neonatal unit as a paediatric registrar, grade ST3, for the whole time. In June 2015 I had been qualified as a doctor for 5 years and working in paediatrics for 2 years and 10 months."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Beech says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I first met [Babies A & B] on 7 June 2015 when I was on the oncall shift, 8.30 am to 21.00 hours (9 pm). I attended their delivery, which was by emergency caesarean section with my senior house officers colleagues, Dr Emily Thomas and Dr Kate Lyddon, along with Staff Nurse Caroline Bennion from the neonatal nursing team. Our attendance was required because it was a twin delivery under general anaesthetic and they, the babies, were premature at 31 weeks and 2 days' gestation.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have been present at many deliveries of babies prior to this, including a large number via emergency caesarean section, many of which were under general anaesthesia, many preterm deliveries and some deliveries of twins and triplets, so this was not something I was unfamiliar with.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As [Baby A] was twin (sic), I asked Dr Thomas and Dr Lyddon to stabilise his sister, who was twin 1."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It should read "as [Baby A] was twin 2".
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As [Baby A] was a twin, I asked..."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It does read that, sorry. My mistake:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As [Baby A] was a twin, I asked Dr Thomas and Dr Lyddon to stabilise his sister, who was twin 1, after her delivery and I said I, as the registrar, would manage [Baby A] as he was twin 2. And it is well-known that often the second twin needs more assistance than the first. I asked Staff Nurse Bennion to assist me in case more than one pair of hands was needed. I had checked the resuscitation equipment in theatre prior to [Baby A] being born and was satisfied that all I may require was available and working correctly.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The caesarean section would have been carried out by members of the obstetric team. After delivery, the babies would then have been passed to a midwife who brings them each to a Resuscitaire. In general, at a delivery, there is often two obstetric doctors, a scrub nurse, at least one anaesthetist, at least one midwife, and at least one healthcare assistant, along with the neonatal team.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby A] was born at 20.31 hours in the theatre on the labour ward. He was brought from his mother to the Resuscitaire, where I was waiting for him, which would have been next to the wall in theatre in order to provide it with power, oxygen and suction.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "A Resuscitaire is a table with a soft mattress, with towels on, with an overhead heater, a clock, which is very important as you start the timer as soon as the baby is born, oxygen, and other equipment which may be required to stabilise a newborn, such as gloves, stethoscopes and endotracheal tubes. They are in all labour rooms as well as theatre.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby A] was brought to me, wrapped in a NeoWrap, which is a plastic sheet into which babies born at less than 32 weeks' gestation are put, in order to keep them warm and moist.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I assessed him in the way in which all newborns are assessed at birth. He had good tone, meaning he was not floppy. He was blue/pink in colour, which is normal for a baby who has just been born. I listened for a heartbeat, but was unable to hear one. [Baby A] showed some signs of breathing, but these were minimal and not enough for him not to require any assistance.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As per the neonatal life support guidelines, I gave [Baby A] five inflation breaths using a Neopuff face mask over his mouth and nose in order to inflate his lungs.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: With each of these breaths, there was no adequate chest wall movement seen, as would be expected if these breaths were effective at pushing air into his lungs.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: However, after these breaths, I reassessed for a heartbeat and could now hear it at approximately 40 beats per minute, which is low.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Chest compressions were not commenced at this time as I felt that I had not yet inflated [Baby A]'s lungs adequately and that, if I could, his heart rate would hopefully improve, as I had been taught on the neonatal life support course and seen in practice multiple times previously. Therefore, as per the neonatal life support guidelines, I gave [Baby A] a further five inflation breaths but his chest wall movement was still poor.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I therefore increased the pressure of the breaths I was giving him.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "With these breaths at a higher PIP, much better chest wall movement was seen and [Baby A] became pinker, showing that his blood was being oxygenated. Staff Nurse Bennion increased the oxygen given from air gradually to 80% during me giving these breaths.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby A]'s heart rate when next reassessed after this had come up to above 100 beats per minute, which is within the normal range. After these breaths, he gave a short cry and was breathing regularly by himself following this, by which time he was 4 minutes old."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr Driver, but there's been a strike through the sentence before the one that begins:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "With these breaths at a higher PIP, much better chest wall movements..."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In fact this was the third lot. The previous sentence says she gave five more breaths at the higher pressure and it was with these that the breathing increased.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That will be recorded on the data, on the iPad.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Your Lordship is quite right to make it plain to the jury that there are three sets of assisted breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, two at the lower pressure, then she increased the pressure and that --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Did the job.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Exactly, got him breathing properly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When he was stimulated by rubbing, he cried and was vigorous in his movements, both of which are good signs.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: However, when he was not stimulated, [Baby A] had some pauses in his breathing, which would not be unexpected for a preterm baby.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As a result of this, I gave him ventilation breaths using the Neopuff face mask, which means that I was ensuring he got adequate oxygen into his lungs when he was not taking a breath for himself. I gave these for a short time before reassessing him again by taking off the face mask. He now had fewer pauses in his breathing, which showed that he was improving.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I therefore held the mask over his mouth and nose so that he was given oxygen and a very small amount of pressure by it, but he was taking all of his breaths by himself. A saturations monitor had been applied by Staff Nurse Bennion and [Baby A] had very good oxygen levels of 95 to 100%. So therefore the amount of oxygen that I was giving him via the face mask was gradually decreased back to room air and [Baby A] was able to maintain good oxygen levels in this.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby A] was fully breathing by himself regularly in air with a small amount of pressure from the face mask by 10 'minutes of age. It is not unexpected that a preterm infant would need to be given some pressure in this way at this age.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: “I assessed [Baby A]'s Apgar scores at being 4 at 1 minute of life, 9 at 5 minutes of life, and 9 at 10 minutes of life. This score is used in order to give people who are not present at the delivery an idea of the condition of the baby at 1, 5 and 10 minutes of age.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The highest possible score is 10. [Baby A]'s Apgar scores are not unusual for a baby born at his gestation and the fact that they were 9 at 5 and 10 minutes show that he responded to initial measures quickly and was in a good condition by these times.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As [Baby A] was a preterm baby, I decided that we should transfer him to the neonatal unit. This was done on the Resuscitaire with me still giving him some pressure via the face mask. [Baby A] had at some point passed urine during the above resuscitation measures.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: His father and grandmother were waiting outside theatre, so I showed [Baby A] to them on the way to the neonatal unit. Transferring [Baby A] to the neonatal unit was the last direct contact that I had with him.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby A] was weighed on arrival in the neonatal unit by members of the nursing team, then transferred to an incubator and put on to CPAP..."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Which we know is continuous airway positive pressure:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "... which is a form of breathing assistance regularly given to preterm infants, which gives them a small amount of pressure into their lungs continuously in order to prevent the small airways from collapsing.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The nursing team set this up and put [Baby A] on to it.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Whilst I documented [Baby A]'s resuscitation, Dr Lyddon inserted a cannula into him in order to be able to give him intravenous medications and took some blood samples from him to look for markers of infection.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This is a standard procedure for a baby of this gestation requiring this level of respiratory support.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My plan for [Baby A] was typical of that for a preterm baby of his gestation born at the Countess of Chester Hospital and one that I have made for several babies previously.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As it was the end of my shift, 21.00 hours, I did not carry out the plan personally but I know that my colleague Dr Lyddon prescribed some of the drugs for [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I ensured that Dr Brunton, who was on for the remainder of the night shift, knew what had happened to [Baby A], as detailed, and where his condition was at currently and also what still needed to be done for him.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After I had finished my documentation of the resuscitation of [Baby A], which I started to do at 21.00 hours, I then left and went home. This was the last physical contact that I had with [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My involvement with [Baby B]. As I have mentioned, myself and Dr Thomas and Dr Lyddon knew we were going into a complicated delivery as it was an emergency caesarean section, twins and premature as well. We sometimes anticipate that the second twin may have more issues than the first and so generally the more senior person will normally take the second twin when they are born. Therefore, for the birth of these twins, Dr Thomas and Dr
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Lyddon took [Baby B], twin 1, after she was delivered. Her brother, [Baby A], was brought over to me and Staff Nurse Bennion and I competed everything that I have already detailed.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As I was dealing with [Baby A], I remember seeing Doctors Thomas and Lyddon doing chest compressions on [Baby B], which alarmed me. By this stage I knew they would have already completed the airway procedures like I had done with [Baby A]. I knew this was a bad sign in that I needed to go over and help as [Baby B] was very unstable, but [Baby A] was also unstable too. It was difficult to know, as the most senior doctor present, which baby I should assist with as I felt [Baby B] was probably more unstable but that [Baby A] was not stable enough for me to leave only with Staff Nurse Bennion.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It was just at this moment that Dr Brunton walked in and asked what was going on and where he was needed.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I immediately told him to help with [Baby B]. I then remained with [Baby A], focusing on him.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I noted an entry in [Baby B]'s notes from Dr Thomas that Dr Saladi arrived when [Baby B] was 14 minutes of age. I cannot remember seeing Dr Saladi as I must have been busy caring for [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I did not have any direct dealing with [Baby B] on this shift. I believe she eventually went into the neonatal unit. After the delivery of [Babies A & B], I came back into work on Tuesday, 9 June 2015. I don't think I was on duty on 8 June 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I next met [Baby B] on 9 June 2015 on the ward round.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I have listed her problems as: prematurity, as she was born at less than 37 weeks' gestation; RDS, which stands for respiratory distress syndrome, because [Baby B] was receiving some help with her breathing. There was a suspected sepsis because she was on antibiotics to cover for a possible infection. And establishing feeds as she was not yet having her full requirement of feeds into her stomach.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I also noted that mum had multiple health issues and that [Baby B] had jaundice. I have also noted that twin 2, [Baby A], had died.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have then listed [Baby B]'s medications. With regard to ventilation, [Baby B] was on CPAP, which is a mask that goes over the nose and provides oxygen and pressure to keep the lungs open. I also examined [Baby B] from top to toe. I would have listened to her lungs with a stethoscope, listened to her heart and her abdomen as well as feeling this.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 8 June, urea and creatine are a little raised.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: There are markers to show -- these are markers to show how your kidneys are working and can be raised if you are dehydrated. There is nothing too concerning, though. The CRP has gone up to 3 but this is still a normal result.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 9 June, urea and creatine have increased further. This is something which needed to be monitored closely."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I think if we look at the screen, the iPad, briefly, on the [Baby B] file, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause)

Slide 57. That's an entry by Dr Gail Beech, the doctor whose statement I'm reading. If we click behind that tile, please. We see the analyst's summary of the notes and her observations. If we go to the underlying note.
My Lord, there are -- although there isn't much of this statement to read, there will be reference to another half a dozen tiles or so.
We'll have a break then.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You're going to be looking at the notes made by the doctor. We're not going to hear from the doctor, obviously, because her statement is being read, so you may have to go through it and just point out... All right. We'll have a 10-minute break then, a comfort break essentially.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Can you be ready, please, to resume at quarter past, which is just over 10 minutes?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (A short break)
My Lord, members of the jury, I was in the process of reading the contents of a statement from Dr Beech, who had taken us up to the care and observations of [Baby B] on 9 June.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Mr Murphy has displayed on the screen now Dr Beech's notes, which lie behind slide 57 on the folder devoted to [Baby B] and I was reading to you Dr Beech's observations. If you look at this document:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The Countess of Chester: weekly neonatal review."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The date, [Baby B]'s gestation age, day 3, consultant's name, and you may recall just before the break I read out to you what Dr Beech had put in the set. The problem list: prematurity, respiratory distress syndrome, suspected sepsis, establishing feeds, multiple maternal problems, and so on.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Beech's statement says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Under abnormal microbiology, I have documented 'BC 33 hours no growth'. This refers to a blood culture, which is a blood sample taken when she was born, which was then sent to the laboratory. And over a period of 36 to 48 hours the lab sees if it grows any bugs, which would also mean that they are present in [Baby B]'s body.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: My documentation means that at 33 hours, the blood sample has not grown any bugs."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So as well as some problems that [Baby B] was having, she'd recorded the feedback from the lab.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The management plan for [Baby B] was to start allowing time off CPAP, to perform a cranial ultrasound scan, complete her baby check, to increase her fluids to 90ml/kg/day, with the aim of giving her more hydration.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I have queried in my plan as to whether [Baby B] can come off her antibiotics and to request a blood test to see if her blood is clotting normally, both of which I have said I will discuss with the consultant. I have then documented that I spoke to Dr Saladi, who was happy for [Baby B] to come off her antibiotics, as both hers and [Baby A]'s blood cultures were negative.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At 10.55 on 9 June I documented a review that was completed by Dr Saladi, where I acted as his scribe."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could now go to slide number 63, please. We see the clinical notes has this doctor's name and the consultant, Dr Saladi. We have the analyst's summary of what we're about to see in the handwritten original that you've already seen previously.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Beech's statement says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Saladi noted that the last blood gas was good and the glucoses [as in blood sugars] on the gases were fine."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: You have seen this and looked at the contents previously. If we could then move, please, to slide number 69, which is Dr Beech's clinical notes at 11.05 on the morning of 9 June. You can see
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: that the doctor has recorded communication with -- you'll become familiar with this -- AHCH, Alder Hey Children's Hospital, which is the surgical unit for the regional neonatal services. That's set out in your agreed facts.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And the feedback from Alder Hey was that [Baby B]'s mother's condition, the syndrome about which there had been some concern earlier, is due to acquired antibodies and should not cross the placenta, ie wouldn't pass to the babies, and therefore not an issue from the view of the experts at Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could then go to slide 85, please. Later, now in the afternoon, 14.50 hours on 9 June, a note of further feedback from the haematology, the blood, special registrar, I think that is, at Alder Hey Children's Hospital, who reported that she, at Alder Hey, had spoken to a couple of her consultants and they have recommended that the Countess send a coagulation screen and D-dimer and they've asked for samples on twin 2, [Baby A], and for an urgent post-mortem of [Baby A], particularly to look for thrombosis, as this may have implications for [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm sure you get the gist of that, members of the jury. The events regarding [Baby A], the tragic events regarding [Baby A], caused the doctors to take special analysis of [Baby B] and monitor her conditions as a precaution.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That is effectively the evidence of Dr Gail Beech in relation to her presence at the delivery and her subsequent care of [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR EMILY THOMAS (read)
Next, my Lord, the statement of Dr Emily Thomas, which is at page 58 of the bundle provided. It's dated 21 November 2017 stating:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I qualified as a doctor in 2011. I have specialist training in paediatrics with the intention of becoming a consultant paediatrician."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Thomas set out the location of her training and stated:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Whilst at Chester I was in my first year of training and when working on the neonatal unit I was not as involved with patient care as the more senior trainees were. It has been a while since working at Chester and I cannot remember the names of all the nurses. Stephen Brearey was the lead neonatal consultant.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At the start of every shift the doctors have a handover process, which is usually led by the registrar. On Sunday, 7 June 2015 I was working and assisted with the delivery of twins,
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby A] and [Baby B]. I remember before they were born I went with a registrar to talk to the mother. I was learning how to counsel parents who were having premature babies about what they should be expecting.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During the delivery, I worked with my registrar, Dr Gail Beech. It was an emergency section and it was a preterm twin delivery. There was a requirement for two doctors to be present. There were neonatal nurses present but I cannot remember who was there.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I took the care of twin 1, which was [Baby B], along with the support of Dr Kate Lyddon. Dr Gail Beech took the care of twin 2, [Baby A], at her Resuscitaire with the support of one of the nursing staff.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby B] was born blue and floppy with a low heart rate. I followed the neonatal life support algorithm and commenced resuscitation, which progressed to CPR due to a persistently low heart rate after I felt I had seen adequate ventilation. I attempted to intubate her at this point but was unsuccessful. The night registrar, Andrew Brunton, took over and continued with the resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her heart rate picked up, although she continued to need respiratory support, and she was transferred to the neonatal unit, intubated and placed in an incubator and on a ventilator. This was my only involvement with [Babies A & B] as their care was handed over to the night team. I was on leave the following week when [Baby A] sadly died.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In September 2015 I moved to Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR ANDREW BRUNTON (read)
Next, my Lord, is a statement from Dr Andrew Brunton, page 62 of your bundle, dated, members of the jury, on 10 April 2018.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: He states that he is a fully registered medical practitioner with the General Medical Council and a member of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I moved to the Mersey Deanery in August 2011 as part of my paediatric training and started at the Liverpool Women's Hospital. The training includes being moved to different hospitals within the area on a 6-month basis. In February 2013 I had my first rotation at the Countess of Chester Hospital as a specialist trainee before moving to Alder Hey Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: In February 2015 I returned to the Countess of Chester Hospital for the second time and remained there until July 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At this time I was a specialist trainee year 4 in paediatrics and my mentor or educational supervisor was [Dr C]. It was a mixture of day and night shifts during this time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In reference to the neonatal unit, nursery 1 is the intensive care room where a sick/premature baby is admitted from the labour ward. It will be allocated a bay within the nursery. The baby would then be assessed, examined and appropriate treatment would then be started.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As the intensity of the baby's care reduces, then it could be moved to one of the side nurseries before being discharged."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, my Lord, the jury were shown, a day or two ago, a walk-through of an empty neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital. We've now recovered and are in a position to play a video recording from within nursery 1, recorded well, well after these events, but at a time when it was still populated.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER
