blocks.text: Witness statement of DR THERESA MacCARRICK (read)

Next, a statement from a Dr Theresa MacCarrick at 70 of your Lordship's bundle. Dr MacCarrick made a statement dated 17 September 2019. She informs us that she has undertaken her paediatric training to date in the Mersey Deanery, the region that we are focusing upon, and confirms that she was asked to provide a statement detailing her involvement in the treatment of [Baby A]:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have had access to a copy of the clinical records and a report that I completed for the coroner to assist me.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was employed at the Countess of Chester Hospital between 4 March and 2 September 2015. During this time my role as senior house officer was a training role and I worked under the supervision of more senior colleagues, a registrar, consultants, and in conjunction with other health professionals, including pharmacists, nursing staff and dieticians. As an SHO I worked across the paediatric, neonatal and post-natal wards.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Typically on the paediatric ward I would attend ward rounds and write up the notes for the leading clinician, who would be a registrar or consultant.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I looked after children admitted to the paediatric ward or assessed patients referred for review by doctors in A&E or GPs.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As the SHO I would usually be the first paediatric doctor to review the new referrals. I would then discuss the case with a senior colleague who will review the patient shortly afterwards. If any treatment or investigations were required whilst waiting for review by a senior, I would instigate these following discussion with the senior. I would also complete ward jobs, including prescriptions and investigations such as blood tests. I would carry out procedures such as inserting cannulas, sometimes with a senior assisting or training me, depending on the complexity of the procedure.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When allocated to the post-natal ward I would complete the first medical examination of the newborn babies, which is a national screening requirement.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I would also review newborn babies who were being treated for suspected sepsis and jaundice. I would always have access to senior support, usually a registrar, and departmental guidelines for help and advice when completing these duties.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When allocated to the neonatal unit, I would write up the ward round for the leading clinician, registrar or consultant. If there was a very stable baby on the unit I would sometimes be asked to complete their daily review by myself. In these circumstances I would update my registrar or consultant with my findings and plan to ensure there was nothing I had missed. I undertook procedures, initially cannulas and lumbar punctures."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Turning to Dr MacCarrick's involvement with [Baby A], she states:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I first met [Baby A] on 8 June 2015. I was on a day shift, 8.30 in the morning until 4.30 in the afternoon. [Baby A] had been assessed on the neonatal ward round at 09.45 on 8 June 2015 during the ward round completed by Dr Ogden. On this particular day I do not recall which area I was allocated to. To the best
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: of my knowledge I had not been allocated to the neonatal unit, but rather was invited to go there in the afternoon because there was an opportunity to gain experience in umbilical line insertion, which was a requirement of my training at that stage.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "To the best of my recollection, it was Sally Ogden, the paediatric registrar, who invited me over to the neonatal unit with the intention of teaching me how to carry out this procedure after she'd completed the neonatal unit ward round.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The reason [Baby A] required the UVC was due to [Baby A] being born prematurely. His gut was not ready to absorb milk in the volumes that he required for nutrition. It would have been safer for [Baby A] to receive total parenteral nutrition (TPN). This is nutrition that is administered through a vein. If TPN is administered through a cannula it can cause problems due to the vein being so small, so the safest way to give TPN is through a central vein. The safest way to gain access to a central vein is to pass a catheter into the umbilical cord via an umbilical venous catheter (UVC). The UVC also provides a reliable way of administering other medication required intravenously, for example antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In a freshly cut umbilical cord three vessels, two arteries and a vein, can be identified. The umbilical vein leads to a much larger vein, the inferior vena cava, which brings blood back to the heart to be pumped through the lungs where it is supplied with oxygen.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Blood is then pumped back round the body, delivering this oxygen to the tissues.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The UVC was inserted under sterile conditions, which is the usual practice, to reduce the risk of infection. Dr Ogden and I completed the procedure together. I inserted the UVC with Dr Ogden and cannot recall any problems or concerns arising during the procedure. [Baby A] would have been covered by a sterile sheet with monitoring equipment attached to him, measuring his heart, oxygen levels, et cetera, and these would have been displayed on a screen next to his incubator. Dr Ogden and I would have been aware of these readings throughout.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby A]'s nurse would have kept records of these numbers periodically. These observations did not indicate any cause for concern with [Baby A]'s condition throughout the procedure.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Inserting a UVC can take a significant amount of time. In addition to the procedure itself there are many steps involved in preparing for the procedure, including collecting all the equipment, scrubbing in, et cetera. Dr Ogden was teaching me and this would have added extra time at each stage. Steps involved
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: in the procedure itself include cutting the umbilical cord, examining the blood vessels and identifying the umbilical vein, passing the catheter into the umbilical vein and then, once the catheter has advanced to the required distance, then checking that blood can be aspirated [ie drawn back in a syringe] from the catheter. This indicates that it, the catheter, is in a large vein, and then flushing the catheter with saline.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Once sited, the UVC needs to be secured in place.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: In essence, this involves taking a needle and thread and stitching through the jelly part of the cord, then wrapping the thread around the catheter in a ballet shoe style with multiple knots. This part of the procedure can take a long time, especially for a trainee who is learning the skill.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Once the UVC has been inserted a portable chest and abdominal X-ray was requested to assess the position of [Baby A]'s UVC. This is the standard method of checking the UVC position."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The intended position for a UVC was the inferior vena cava. However, as UVC insertion is a blind procedure, the catheter can deviate to one side. A UVC catheter deviating into the hepatic circulation is a common complication in this procedure. It is my usual practice to wait with the baby until the X-ray is completed and the line position can be assessed."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could please go to [Baby A] on the screen and go to slide 128.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: 128. We can see the name of Dr Anne Boothroyd again, the consultant radiologist. If we click behind, please. Confirmation that an X-ray was taken. We have the analyst's summary of what was seen:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The heart size was normal. Improved aeration of both lungs. Tiny traces of fluid in the horizontal fissure was resolved, suggesting this was at least partly due to transient tachypnoeia of the newborn. The tip of the nasogastric tube is projected over the body of the stomach. The tip of the UVC lies 12 millimetres proximal to the junction. However, it is a medial curvature, suggesting it may lie in the left blanche of the portal vein. The bowel gas pattern is within normal limits for the baby's age."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That sets all that out. If we go to the main page, please, a slide 134. We'll see on the chronology, 134 is the review that I'm about to tell you about:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Ogden and I [it says Dr MacCarrick] reviewed the X-ray. The UVC appeared to be sited in the hepatic circulation."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: We see on our screen a reference to liver. That's the same thing:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "So it is there in the hepatic circulation rather than the intended position in the IVC. Dr Ogden and I sought advice from the responsible paediatric consultant, Dr Jayaram."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So we see in abbreviated form:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Discussed with Dr Ogden and Dr Jayaram."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram had just finished his clinic and was in the vicinity:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Jayaram agreed that the UVC had deviated from its intended course and appeared to be sited in the hepatic circulation. When this happens, it is standard practice to take the UVC out and straightaway replace it with a new catheter, which is what Dr Jayaram advised us to do.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I returned to the neonatal unit to remove the original UVC and replace it immediately as advised by Dr Jayaram. This was again completed under sterile conditions. On this second occasion I worked independently without direct supervision. This had been agreed between me, Dr Ogden and Dr Jayaram. Dr Ogden was the only registrar on shift that day and was required to go to the paediatric ward to review some patients. I felt confident to complete the procedure independently on this second occasion. Even though I had only just completed the procedure myself for the first time, I had observed colleagues inserting UVCs many times previously and was aware of the steps and important precautions.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The paediatric ward where Dr Ogden needed to go is located next to the neonatal unit and she was easily contactable if I encountered any difficulties."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could go, please, to slide 143. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Just click on to Dr MacCarrick's notes. So recording in brief that which I've just read out in more detail.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Going back to Dr MacCarrick's statement, if I may:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Once I had inserted a new UVC, a repeat chest and abdominal Xray were requested to assess its position.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: On inspection of the repeat X-ray, the UVC again appeared to me to be situated in the hepatic circulation rather than the IVC."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr MacCarrick requested Dr Ogden and Dr Harkness to review the X-ray with her. If we then go to slide 144, please and we go to the underlying notes, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: You'll be familiar with this sort of page, members of the jury. You can see an X-ray review comes on -- you'll hear some doctors refer to it as a sticker that should be placed on to the notes. It's a distinctive red typeface. We see Dr Ogden's signature at the bottom. The time of the X-ray, the date of the X-ray and the comments on the position, et cetera, of the feature being examined and then the comment as to what should happen. Then we have some contribution from Dr Harkness below.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Going back to Dr MacCarrick's statement, she requested Dr Ogden and Dr Harkness review the X-ray with her. They agreed with Dr MacCarrick's impression that the UVC appeared to be in the hepatic vein and that [Baby A] would need a long line, as previously discussed with the consultant, Dr Jayaram:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At this time [Baby A] remained in the neonatal unit being monitored by the nurses and the inserted UVC would not have been used. It is standard procedure not to use a UVC until it has been confirmed to be in the correct position on an X-ray."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So more than one attempt, not successful, and therefore not used for the purpose for which it was inserted in the first place:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I did not return to the neonatal unit to remove the UVC after this discussion as both Dr Ogden and Dr Harkness assured me that, as I had already stayed beyond the end of my shift, I could go home and they would complete all remaining jobs. I left the hospital some time after 5 pm, leaving [Baby A] in the care of Dr Harkness and Dr Ogden. I had no concerns regarding [Baby A]'s clinical condition at any point during the insertion or replacement of the UVC. This was the last contact I had with [Baby A]. I heard that [Baby A] had passed away when I came back into work the following day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember worrying that anything to do with the UVC insertion attempts could have been connected to [Baby A]'s death. The first promise of the Hippocratic Oath is to do no harm and wondering whether my procedure could have done anything to damage [Baby A] or cause his death was upsetting. I always feel sad when a patient I have treated passes away and I always reflect on whether anything could have been done differently to save them. Despite being reassured by several colleagues that my UVC was very unlikely to have anything to do with [Baby A]'s death, I was not 100% reassured until I reviewed the examination findings of [Baby A]'s post-mortem examination."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It's actually "several senior colleagues".

blocks.text: "Several senior colleagues", forgive me.

Witness statement of DR SALLY OGDEN (read)
Members of the jury, may I continue to read some evidence, this time a statement from a Dr Sally Ogden.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Ogden made a statement on 6 February 2018, detailing her involvement in the care of [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Ogden confirmed that she had been given access to a copy of the clinical records to assist her in her recollections and that the account is written from a review of those medical records and from her personal recollection.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Ogden stated:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I first met [Baby A] on 8 June 2015 when I was working a standard day shift between 8.30 am and 16.30, ie 4.30 pm, as a paediatric registrar on the children's ward of the neonatal unit. Dr David Harkness returned from his other commitments out in the community to take over as a paediatric registrar from 16.30 hours to complete the rest of the long day until 20.30 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby A] is also referred to as [Baby A]. The reasons for this are all babies born in hospital are registered under their mother's surname. This is to make sure both sets of case notes marry up and to avoid any confusion.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At the beginning of each day a ward round is conducted. On 8 June 2015, I was the paediatric registrar on duty. I was in company with senior house officer Theresa MacCarrick. Part of the ward round is to assess each individual baby on the neonatal unit. As the paediatric registrar I would have assessed the
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: babies in the intensive care unit. I reviewed [Baby A] on the unit at 09.45 hours on 8 June 2015."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If I could ask Mr Murphy to put up slide 84, please, we can see Dr Ogden's name.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go behind that slide, we have the analyst's description of what it was that Dr Ogden noted in her clinical notes. If we could go to Dr Ogden's underlying notes, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: You can see her name on the top line. 09.45 on 8 June, ST3, specialist trainee 3, S Ogden. It records that [Baby A] was twin number 2. This is day 2 of his life. He hadn't(?) been born after 31 weeks and 2 days.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll leave that on the screen and I'll go back to Dr Ogden's statement about the assessment made at 09.45 on 8 June:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The assessment is conducted to establish the clinical management of each baby, to identify any immediate medical requirements and to assess the baby's level of respiratory support (do they require intubating, assistance with CPAP)? Is intravenous access required? Are they having antibiotics? Are fluids levels correct? These are just some of the considerations made during my assessment on each baby during the ward round.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "From memory, I do not recall anything particular out of the ordinary with either [Baby A] or [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I would have reviewed their clinical and medical needs during the morning ward round. From memory, I recall [Baby B] was slightly more unstable than [Baby A], but without reviewing her medical notes I am unable to go into detail.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I recall they both required long lines putting in to provide nutrients in a more secure way. At the time they both had intravenous access and there was no immediate concern. If there were any immediate medical concerns I would have expected them to have been highlighted during the handover and discussed during the ward round or, if they required immediate attention, an emergency crash call would have been put out.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "From the ward round on the neonatal unit that morning, I would have created a list of jobs that required completing. Any urgent jobs would have been done at the time."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The statement goes on and this reflects the note on screen:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Babies A & B] were preterm twins who had been born the previous day at 31 weeks and 2 days' gestation. They were both 12 hours old.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After reviewing [Baby A], my plan was to keep him on continuous positive airway pressure ventilation but start to feed him. He needed a central line for ongoing parenteral nutrition and needed a cranial ultrasound performing. He needed repeated blood tests taken later on 8 June 2015 to check his renal function, Creactive protein and bilirubin level. [Baby A] had a peripheral venous cannula for intravenous access."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Moving on in time now:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During the afternoon of 8 June 2015 myself and Dr Theresa MacCarrick, who at the time was an ST1 paediatric trainee, inserted an umbilical venous catheter with aseptic technique to 8 centimetres of length. I was teaching Dr MacCarrick how to perform this procedure and we jointly performed this procedure under my supervision. I reviewed the position of the umbilical venous catheter on the abdominal X-ray."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll go to it very quickly because we've already looked at it. Go to slide 142, please. We've already heard Dr MacCarrick, through her statement, speak of this. This was the X-ray taken by Dr Anne Boothroyd that Monday afternoon, 8 June 2015. Then if we go forward to slide 144, we see the joint X-ray review taken by Dr Ogden in the company of Dr MacCarrick. So there we have Dr Ogden's note, timed at 17.00, written in retrospect, recording how the UVC was earlier inserted, using the aseptic technique, the sterile technique, to 8 centimetres, and how it was X-rayed and the result of the X-ray and the consequential action.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So going back, if I may, to Dr Ogden's statement:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I reviewed the position of the umbilical venous catheter on the abdominal X-ray with Dr Jayaram, the paediatric consultant on call. The X-ray showed it positioned in the hepatic vein. I remember going into clinic and interrupting Dr Jayaram to show him [Baby A]'s X-ray. After liaising with Dr Jayaram we both agreed that the line was not in a satisfactory position. His advice was to remove the umbilical venous catheter and replace it with a new catheter to try and position it in the inferior vena cava.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was the only paediatric registrar in the department on the afternoon of 8 June 2015 and at this particular point in time I had been asked to review a patient on the children's paediatric ward."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So Dr Ogden was the only registrar in the department and she'd been asked to do something else:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I approached Dr Theresa MacCarrick and asked her if she was happy to take out the umbilical venous catheter and insert a new one under aseptic technique by herself using the technique I had shown her earlier. She informed me she was able to do this while I reviewed the child on the children's ward."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go to slide 144, please. 145. Thank you. So we have a note from Dr Ogden, timed at 17.00 hours, but written in retrospect. To give context to this and from Dr Ogden's statement:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At 16.00 hours on 8 June 2015 I handed over to the evening registrar, Dr Harkness, who had returned from his other commitments. During handover, I once again reviewed the X-ray of the new umbilical venous catheter that had been inserted by Dr MacCarrick. This showed that the catheter was still sited within the hepatic vein. I asked Dr Harkness to remove this umbilical venous catheter and to insert a peripheral long line instead into [Baby A]. It was around the same time I was informed by one of the neonatal nursing staff that [Baby A]'s peripheral cannula had tissued. This was the line that [Baby A] was receiving his nutrition through and therefore it had become slightly more urgent during the handover. I informed Dr Harkness of this.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After handing over the evening jobs to Dr Harkness, I went back to the neonatal unit at 17.00 hours to retrospectively document the events of the afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This was due to workload as I had not yet documented it in the notes."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So hence the retrospective note on screen timed at 17.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could go to the underlying note, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER
